title: 6. 10-Year Financial Forensics, Cash Conversion & Balance Sheet

epigraph.quote: As a result, free cash flow improved markedly during the year, moving from Rs. (4.85) Cr in FY25 to Rs. (0.09) Cr in FY26.
epigraph.author: SoftTech Engineers Ltd, Annual Report 2025-26, Management Discussion and Analysis, section 8.3 (standalone free cash flow)

web_blocks.html: Start with the number people argue about. For the year to 31 March 2026, SoftTech's audited consolidated profit after tax was ₹5.33 crore, of which ₹4.94 crore belongs to the parent's shareholders. The standalone company, meaning the Pune parent on its own without its nine subsidiaries, earned ₹9.57 crore [27][28]. Both are right. They measure different perimeters, and FY2026 has no exceptional item in either. The only exceptional charge in the recent record is a ₹0.78 crore impairment of the Finland subsidiary in FY2025, and it appears only in the standalone accounts [27]. Some third-party pages carry a standalone FY2026 profit of about ₹18.8 crore. It matches nothing in the filed statements, where standalone profit before tax is ₹12.99 crore, profit after tax ₹9.57 crore and total comprehensive income ₹6.44 crore [27]. I treat it as wrong.

The same split explains the latest quarter. For Q2 FY2027, the three months to 30 September 2026, consolidated profit was ₹0.21 crore (₹0.11 crore to owners) and standalone profit was ₹3.63 crore [30]. Aggregator headlines of ₹0.21 crore are quoting the consolidated line [38]; the ₹3.63 crore is the standalone line of the same filing. Neither is a typo and neither is the 'real' profit. For a shareholder in the listed company, the consolidated figure is the honest one, because it includes every rupee the group spends, including on its overseas start-ups.

web_blocks.caption: Standalone versus consolidated: FY2026 (audited) and Q2 FY2027 (unaudited); ₹ crore unless stated
rows: Purchases of traded software, net of stock change
web_blocks.takeaway: Source: audited FY2026 statements and the unaudited Q2 FY2027 filing; percentages are my arithmetic on filed figures [27][30]. Purchases are identical in both columns because the traded-software business sits wholly in the parent.

web_blocks.html: Read the gap line by line. In FY2026 the subsidiaries added ₹4.60 crore of revenue but ₹5.47 crore of employee cost and ₹1.34 crore of other expense. The parent's other income of ₹5.49 crore, which includes ₹0.57 crore of interest on debentures it holds in its own subsidiaries and ₹1.68 crore of foreign-exchange gains, shrinks to ₹3.64 crore on consolidation. So ₹12.99 crore of standalone pre-tax profit becomes ₹8.93 crore [27]. In Q2 FY2027 consolidated revenue is even ₹1.17 crore below standalone; the filing does not say why, and intra-group billing eliminated on consolidation is my likely reading [30].

The tax line is the real oddity. Tax is paid by the parent on its own profit, so consolidated tax (₹3.60 crore) is almost the same as standalone tax (₹3.41 crore) even though group profit is ₹4.06 crore lower. The consolidated tax note says so in plain words: ₹1.21 crore of FY2026 tax, and ₹1.48 crore in FY2025, is 'non-creation of deferred tax on losses in subsidiaries' [27]. Losses in the overseas companies earn no tax credit because the group has not booked a future benefit for them. That is why the effective rate is 40% in FY2026, 59% in FY2025 and 77% in Q2 FY2027, against 26% for the parent alone [27][30]. The same pattern shows in FY2023 (44%) and FY2024 (41%) [33][32]. It is not a trick. It is the cost of running loss-making start-ups inside a profitable Indian parent, and it will stay until those subsidiaries earn money.

Now the long arc, ten years. The 2018 annual report is standalone only: revenue of ₹46.7 crore in FY2017 and ₹51.5 crore in FY2018, profit after tax ₹4.9 crore and ₹6.8 crore, under the old Indian accounting rules [36]. The feed's consolidated series starts in FY2019 at about ₹63 crore of revenue and ₹7 crore of profit [37]. FY2020 was ₹57.95 crore and ₹6.49 crore [35]. Then the pandemic year: revenue fell 28% to ₹41.6 crore in FY2021, and profit, restated to Ind AS, was ₹2.58 crore [34]. Recovery followed: ₹57.5 crore in FY2022, ₹65.4 crore in FY2023, ₹78.8 crore in FY2024, ₹95.2 crore in FY2025 and ₹132.9 crore in FY2026 [34][33][32][31][27]. Revenue is 3.2 times FY2021 and 2.1 times FY2019. Profit has not followed. Consolidated profit after tax for FY2022 to FY2026 was ₹4.65 crore, ₹3.62 crore, ₹3.32 crore, ₹1.33 crore and ₹5.33 crore, a five-year total of ₹18.25 crore on ₹430 crore of cumulative revenue [34][33][32][31][27].

web_blocks.caption: SoftTech Engineers: consolidated profit-and-loss history (feed, rounded), FY2019 to TTM
web_blocks.takeaway: Sales roughly doubled between FY2019 and FY2026 while operating margin sat in a 24% to 30% band. Depreciation climbs from ₹4 crore to ₹23 crore and absorbs almost all of the gain, which is why net profit stays in single digits. TTM is a rolling twelve months, not an audited year.

web_blocks.html: Here is the FY2026 margin bridge per ₹100 of consolidated revenue. Purchases of traded software, net of stock change, cost ₹14.5. Employees cost ₹24.8. Other expenses cost ₹36.5, a line that holds ₹9.4 of credit-loss provision (₹12.49 crore) and, in the parent, ₹22.24 crore of outsourced technical consultants, up from ₹13.96 crore [27]. What remains is EBITDA of ₹24.2, or ₹32.19 crore, which is earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation. Depreciation and amortisation take ₹17.2. Interest takes ₹3.1. Other income adds ₹2.7. Pre-tax profit is ₹6.7. The feed's waterfall tells the same story in rounded form [37].

The margin did not improve in eight years. EBITDA margin was 25% in FY2019 and 24% in FY2026 [37]. What changed is below that line. Depreciation and amortisation rose from ₹4 crore, about 6% of revenue, in FY2019 to ₹22.8 crore, 17%, in FY2026, so pre-tax margin fell from about 17% to 6.7% [37][27]. Interest is the smaller drag. Finance cost was ₹4.07 crore in FY2026: ₹3.18 crore on borrowings and ₹0.71 crore on lease liabilities in the parent [27]. EBITDA covers that 7.9 times. EBIT, which is EBITDA less depreciation and amortisation and before other income, covers it only 2.3 times.

Why does amortisation keep climbing? SoftTech writes its own software, the Civit suite for building permits, infrastructure and construction. Under Ind AS 38 it capitalises eligible development cost, meaning it records the spend as an asset instead of an expense, and amortises it straight-line over four years once the product is available for use. Until then the money sits in 'intangible assets under development' [27]. The auditor makes this a key audit matter 'due to the significant value of the development costs', and the notes concede that 'there is significant management judgement and estimate involved' in deciding which costs qualify [27]. In FY2026 ₹36.48 crore went into the under-development account, ₹33.05 crore moved into finished software and ₹20.43 crore of internally generated software was amortised [27]. Put those next to EBITDA and you see how much of 'operating profit' is really re-invested engineering.

web_blocks.caption: What if the engineering had been expensed? Consolidated, ₹ crore
headers: Development cost capitalised in the year
web_blocks.takeaway: Source: filed consolidated profit-and-loss accounts and the intangible-asset notes for each year [33][32][31][27]. Last column = reported profit less capitalised cost plus the amortisation that would no longer be charged. EBITDA is computed as revenue less purchases, stock change, employee and other expenses.

web_blocks.html: Read the last column with care. It is a sensitivity, not a restatement. Some capitalised cost is genuine asset-building, and the notes do not split capitalised salary from contractor cost, so I cannot say how much would have been an expense in a stricter regime. But the direction is clear: in FY2024, FY2025 and FY2026 the group would have reported a pre-tax loss had it expensed development as it went. Cash tells the same tale. Across FY2022 to FY2026 the group paid ₹117.16 crore for intangibles against cumulative EBITDA of ₹110.45 crore [34][33][32][31][27].

And the pile is growing. Software under development rose from ₹19.56 crore in March 2026 to ₹42.66 crore in September 2026, while finished software fell from ₹70.65 crore to ₹58.18 crore [27][30]. If that ₹42.66 crore entered service on a four-year life it would add about ₹10.7 crore a year of amortisation, against Q2 FY2027 EBITDA of ₹7.98 crore for the quarter and depreciation and amortisation already at ₹6.85 crore [30]. That is arithmetic, not a forecast: it assumes no new revenue from those products. It is why I watch the amortisation line more closely than the EBITDA line.

web_blocks.caption: SoftTech Engineers: consolidated balance sheet history (feed, rounded), FY2019 to September 2026
web_blocks.takeaway: Fixed assets and CWIP in the feed lump software under development with finished software; in September 2026 the feed's ₹111 crore of fixed assets includes ₹42.66 crore under development. Borrowings in the feed include lease liabilities. Net worth is now carried largely by capitalised code and unbilled revenue.

web_blocks.html: Look at what the March 2026 balance sheet holds. Total consolidated assets are ₹253.54 crore. Capitalised software is ₹70.65 crore, software under development ₹19.56 crore, trade receivables ₹34.63 crore and unbilled contract assets ₹53.52 crore. Those four lines are ₹178.4 crore, 70% of everything the group owns [27]. Plant and equipment is just ₹3.62 crore. This is an asset-light business whose assets are code and promises of payment. Goodwill is nil: the only goodwill ever created, ₹0.16 crore on buying the German company, was written off in full in the year of purchase [27].

Investments tell a second story. The parent has put about ₹28.1 crore into subsidiaries, ₹13.7 crore of equity and ₹14.4 crore of optionally convertible debentures [27]. In FY2026 it injected ₹11.25 crore into SoftTech Digital AG, the German company, which in its first months produced no revenue and a ₹0.63 crore loss [27]. Provisions of ₹0.74 crore already sit against subsidiary investments, mostly the Finland debentures [27]. A loss that never touched profit also deserves a mention: the parent's stake in QI Square Singapore was marked down from ₹4.60 crore to ₹1.29 crore, a ₹3.31 crore hit taken through other comprehensive income and so absent from the profit figures above [27]. One consolidation quirk too. Group cash of ₹12.71 crore at March 2026 looks like a ₹10.1 crore rise, but the parent held only ₹1.16 crore. The German subsidiary has ₹10.57 crore of assets against ₹11.35 crore of share capital, so the 'increase' is mostly money moved from the parent's fixed deposits to Germany, not new cash [27].

web_blocks.caption: Borrowings, leases and liquidity; ₹ crore
rows: Bank working-capital loans (secured on receivables and stock)
Loans from promoter-directors (10%, no repayment schedule)
Cash, bank deposits and mutual funds (consolidated)
web_blocks.takeaway: Source: borrowings note 16 and other-financial-liabilities note of the FY2026 annual report; September 2026 totals from the unaudited consolidated balance sheet [27][30]. The loan split is for the parent; its total equals the consolidated total to within ₹0.01 crore.

web_blocks.html: Gross debt barely moved, ₹34.4 crore to ₹31.7 crore, but look at the mix. Seventy-two percent (₹22.93 crore) is bank working-capital lines secured on receivables and stock and backed by personal guarantees and equitable mortgages on the managing director's and his wife's flats [27]. ₹3.02 crore is loans from those two directors at 10%. The non-bank lenders charge about 11.25%, bank lines 7.7% to 10.25% [27]. So the group pays 8% to 11% for money it needs mainly because customers pay slowly. Net of liquid funds it had ₹4.06 crore of net cash at March 2026 before leases and ₹3.03 crore of net debt after them; by September 2026 liquid funds of ₹28.06 crore were below borrowings of ₹32.12 crore [27][30]. Two debt-like items sit outside that table: ₹13.43 crore owed to suppliers for capital purchases, up from ₹7.90 crore, and ₹6.22 crore of fixed deposits pledged to lenders [27]. Contingent liabilities, disputes not provided for, total ₹5.10 crore: ₹3.63 crore of income-tax demands (chiefly a ₹2.75 crore reopening of assessment year 2018-19), ₹1.39 crore of GST and ₹0.08 crore other. Management expects no material cash outflow [27].

web_blocks.caption: Receivables and unbilled revenue at year-end; consolidated, ₹ crore
web_blocks.takeaway: Source: consolidated balance sheets in the FY2022 to FY2026 annual reports and the Sep 2026 filing [34][33][32][31][27][30]; days = (trade receivables + contract assets) ÷ revenue × 365, my arithmetic; debtor-days column from the feed [37].

web_blocks.html: Now the part that matters most. Receivables come in two pieces. Trade receivables are invoices already sent. Contract assets, also called unbilled revenue, are revenue booked under percentage-of-completion accounting but not yet invoiced. Add them and you get what customers owe or will owe: ₹88.15 crore at March 2026 on ₹132.90 crore of revenue, or 242 days. That is down from 628 days in FY2021 and 366 in FY2025 [34][31][27]. Management's own figure for the standalone company is 260 days, down from 462 in FY2022, and the annual report sets a goal of 'bringing DSO below 200 days' [27]. The feed's 95 debtor days covers trade receivables alone and misses the larger half. Its cash-conversion cycle of minus 256 and minus 108 days for FY2025 and FY2026 is an artefact of netting a large payables balance against a small purchases base; ignore it [37].

Who owes it? The filings do not split receivables between government bodies and private customers. The annual report says only that revenue is 'concentrated in a single customer type (government)' [27], and I could not size that exposure. What is disclosed: ₹1.79 crore is owed by the Dubai subsidiary, up from ₹0.74 crore [27]. A municipality that approves a budget in one year and pays in the next is slow money, and the ageing below shows it.

web_blocks.caption: Ageing of gross trade receivables and loss allowance; parent, ₹ crore
web_blocks.takeaway: Source: note 10 (trade receivables ageing) of the FY2026 annual report [27]. Nothing is shown as 'not due' or 'disputed'; every rupee is classed as undisputed and good.

web_blocks.html: The ageing is the uncomfortable part. Of ₹40.83 crore of gross trade receivables, ₹17.28 crore (42%) is more than a year old and ₹4.97 crore is older than three years. The allowance covers 72% of the oldest bucket but only 12% of the one-to-two-year bucket, so cover on everything over a year is 31% [27]. On the unbilled side there is ₹64.89 crore of gross contract assets with an ₹11.37 crore loss allowance, up from ₹2.04 crore. Together the group holds ₹17.65 crore of allowances against ₹105.72 crore of billed and unbilled claims, 16.7%, up from ₹5.16 crore a year earlier [27]. The FY2026 charge of ₹12.49 crore compares with consolidated pre-tax profit of ₹8.93 crore. Bad debt is not new: the annual reports show write-offs of ₹0.92 crore in FY2018 and ₹0.37 crore in FY2021 [36][35]. What is new is the scale, and the timing: parent other expenses jumped to ₹24.80 crore in Q4 against ₹7.87 crore in Q3 [28].

web_blocks.caption: SoftTech Engineers: working-capital and return ratios (feed), FY2019 to FY2026
web_blocks.takeaway: Debtor days and working-capital days improved sharply in FY2026, but the feed counts trade receivables only; unbilled contract assets are in 'other assets'. The negative cash-conversion cycle is a formula artefact, and ROCE is single digits.

web_blocks.html: Returns on capital are the verdict on all of this. The feed's ROCE, operating profit after depreciation over capital employed, was 13% in FY2020 and 6% in FY2026, with 4% in FY2025 [37]. Here is my own version for FY2026, consolidated. EBIT of ₹9.36 crore (pre-tax profit plus interest, less other income), taxed at the 25.17% statutory rate, gives net operating profit after tax of ₹7.01 crore. Invested capital, meaning equity plus borrowings plus leases less cash and liquid funds, averages ₹171.0 crore. Return on invested capital is 4.1%. Add back the credit-loss charge and it is 9.6% [27]. The company's own lenders charge 7.7% to 11.25%, so a 4.1% return does not cover even the cost of debt. A sensible hurdle for the equity of a small Indian software company is 12% to 15%; that is my assumption, not a filed number. Return on equity was 2.9% on owners' equity (management quotes 3.1% on total equity, and 5.2% for the parent alone) [27], and the feed puts the three-year average near 2.1% [37].

web_blocks.caption: SoftTech Engineers: consolidated cash flow history (feed, rounded), FY2019 to FY2026
web_blocks.takeaway: Operating cash flow looks healthy against EBITDA in recent years, but investing outflow, mostly capitalised software, matches or exceeds it. Free cash flow is negative in all eight years, and net cash flow in the later years leans on equity raised and fixed deposits redeemed.

web_blocks.html: Cash flow is where the story turns. Consolidated operating cash flow was ₹31.26 crore in FY2026, nearly six times profit after tax and 97% of EBITDA [27]. Do not applaud yet. Operating cash flow is struck before the cash spent on software development, which the accounts file under investing. Subtract that and free cash flow, operating cash less money spent on equipment and capitalised development, was minus ₹1.30 crore. The feed shows free cash flow negative in every one of the eight years from FY2019 to FY2026, adding to about minus ₹46 crore [37]. Warren Buffett wrote in Berkshire Hathaway's 2000 annual report: 'References to EBITDA make us shudder - does management think the tooth fairy pays for capital expenditures?' Capitalised software is that question in a new costume.

web_blocks.caption: Audited consolidated cash bridge, FY2026 versus FY2025; ₹ crore
rows: Non-cash today, revenue that may never turn into cash
FY26: contract assets and stock absorbed 12.72
- Cash paid for plant and equipment
Before interest paid and lease payments
web_blocks.takeaway: Source: audited consolidated statements of cash flows, FY2026 annual report [27]; subtotals are my arithmetic and tie to the filed totals.

web_blocks.html: The bridge shows what lifted FY2026 operating cash. The ₹12.98 crore credit-loss add-back is 28% of cash earnings before working capital; it is not cash, but it is also a confession that earlier revenue did not convert. Working capital then absorbed ₹10.46 crore: trade receivables released ₹5.60 crore, but contract assets and stock absorbed ₹12.72 crore and payables fell ₹7.13 crore [27]. After the ₹3.44 crore of interest and ₹1.79 crore of lease payments that sit in financing, the shortfall was ₹6.5 crore. The group met it by redeeming a net ₹15.7 crore of fixed deposits, which had been built up in FY2025 when the December 2024 equity issue came in [27]. In the first half of FY2027 operating cash was ₹15.86 crore against ₹22.08 crore spent on development and equipment, a ₹6.23 crore shortfall (₹11.05 crore a year earlier), and the group drew ₹8.92 crore of new term loans [30].

web_blocks.caption: Five-year cash ledger; consolidated, ₹ crore
web_blocks.takeaway: Source: consolidated cash-flow statements and profit-and-loss accounts in the FY2022 to FY2026 annual reports [34][33][32][31][27]. EBITDA and the ratio are my arithmetic. 'New equity raised' is the cash-flow line for share and warrant proceeds.

web_blocks.html: Who funded the gap? Over FY2022 to FY2026, EBITDA of ₹110.45 crore became ₹96.92 crore of operating cash, 88%. The group then spent ₹122.92 crore on development and equipment, a ₹26.0 crore hole before ₹20.33 crore of finance cost. New shareholder money was ₹83.35 crore. Borrowings did not fund it: consolidated debt was ₹32.08 crore at March 2021 and ₹31.74 crore at March 2026 [34][27]. Customers certainly did not. They are the ones being funded, to the tune of ₹88 crore of unpaid claims. The growth of the last five years was paid for by outside equity investors.

web_blocks.caption: Share count and equity raised since the 2018 listing
rows: IPO on NSE SME (fresh issue; a further 4,80,000 shares were sold by an existing investor)
Identified investors (not named in the report)
web_blocks.takeaway: Source: annual reports FY2018, FY2022, FY2023, FY2024, FY2025 and FY2026 [36][34][33][32][31][27]. Issue prices are historic subscription prices set by the issues, not market quotations.

web_blocks.html: Now per-share arithmetic. Shares outstanding rose from 94,22,476 at the 2018 listing to 1,38,42,138 today, up 47% [36][27]. Consolidated earnings per share in the feed went from ₹7.87 in FY2019 to ₹3.57 in FY2026 [37][27]. Outside investors put in ₹102.3 crore of new equity across the IPO and three placements, while the group earned about ₹34 crore in total over FY2019 to FY2026 on the feed's rounded figures [37]. Where did the issue proceeds go? The statement of deviation says nothing was diverted from the stated objects. Of ₹83.30 crore received across the 2021, 2022 and 2024 issues, ₹68.54 crore was used by March 2026: ₹55.77 crore 'to support the expansion of business in Indian and Overseas market' and ₹12.78 crore for general purposes, with ₹14.76 crore left in mutual funds and fixed deposits [27]. By June 2026 ₹33.14 crore of the ₹33.29 crore 2022 issue was used and ₹26.17 crore of the ₹40.01 crore 2024 issue [29]. 'Expansion' is broad enough to cover capitalised software, and the filings do not break it down. For the 2021 issue the early record is specific: by March 2022 ₹2.54 crore of ₹4.47 crore spent had gone to Civit development [34].

The owners behind the share count have changed. Promoter holding was 32.05% in March 2024, 20.35% in June 2024 and 18.89% since December 2024 [37]. The fall followed a June 2024 agreement under which Vijay Gupta, Udyat Indian Ventures LLP and Covisible Solutions sold 25,00,000 shares, 19.5%, to Einstein Work Pte Ltd, which then also took part of the December 2024 issue [31]. Einstein holds 23.41% today [27]. I found no pledge of promoter shares in the annual report or the feed. What is pledged is ₹6.22 crore of bank deposits and the promoters' personal flats and guarantees for bank lines [27]. Stock options are small: ESOP expense was ₹0.78 crore in FY2026 and ₹1.34 crore in FY2025, and 4,200 options at ₹10 were granted to the new chief financial officer in June 2026 [27][30]. The FY2026 option table does not roll forward cleanly: 60,000 opening plus 35,000 granted less 35,000 shares issued is not the 25,000 reported [27].

Governance deserves a plain list. The auditor, P G Bhagwat LLP, has served since the 30 September 2021 annual meeting [34]. It gave unmodified opinions with two key audit matters for FY2026: revenue on fixed-price contracts and capitalised development cost, the latter marked as a key matter 'for the current year' [27]. The Board reports no qualifications or adverse remarks [27]. The audit report on legal requirements does contain a notable item. Quarterly statements filed with the working-capital banks did not agree with the books: for March 2026 the composite of contract assets, receivables, payables, purchases and sales was ₹240.19 crore in the bank return against ₹256.14 crore in the books, and the December 2025 return ran ₹12.35 crore above the books. Management calls the returns provisional and says it will resubmit if permitted [27]. The secretarial auditor notes one late transfer of ₹10,000 of unpaid dividend to the investor protection fund, 125 days late [27].

Related-party and people items. The managing director drew ₹81.00 lakh of salary, ₹62.22 lakh of non-compete fees and ₹29.81 lakh of interest on his loan to the company in FY2026, ₹1.73 crore in all, equal to 32% of consolidated profit after tax [27]. Another executive director's pay rose from ₹14.46 lakh to ₹80.71 lakh [27]. The chief financial officer resigned in September 2025, a new one joined the next day, and the company secretary resigned in March 2026 [27]. The related-party note lists seven directors, four of them independent, with the managing director also chairman and chief executive [27]. None of this is alarming on its own. Together with the bank-return mismatch, the heavy loss allowance and a new key audit matter, it says controls are still catching up with the company's growth.

So what is the earnings quality, in plain words? Reported profit is thin and soft: ₹5.33 crore on ₹132.90 crore of revenue in FY2026, after a ₹12.49 crore credit-loss charge, and a loss if development spend were expensed. The cash is real at the operating line, where EBITDA converts at 88% to 97% over five years, but every rupee of it and more goes back into building software, so free cash flow is negative year after year. Revenue turns into cash slowly (242 days) and, for a growing slice, not at all. The business is funded by new shareholders, not by customers or lenders. Returns, 4.1% on my arithmetic, are below the cost of money. What would change my mind is two or three consecutive years of positive free cash flow with days outstanding under 200, falling allowances and amortisation growing slower than revenue.

The 2018 annual report is standalone only: revenue of ₹46.7 crore in FY2017 and ₹51.5 crore in FY2018, profit after tax ₹4.9 crore and ₹6.8 crore, under the old Indian accounting rules [36]. The feed's consolidated series starts in FY2019 at about ₹63 crore of revenue and ₹7 crore of profit [37]. FY2020 was ₹57.95 crore and ₹6.49 crore [35]. Then the pandemic year: revenue fell 28% to ₹41.6 crore in FY2021, and profit, restated to Ind AS, was ₹2.58 crore [34]. Recovery followed: ₹57.5 crore in FY2022, ₹65.4 crore in FY2023, ₹78.8 crore in FY2024, ₹95.2 crore in FY2025 and ₹132.9 crore in FY2026 [34][33][32][31][27]. Revenue is 3.2 times FY2021 and 2.1 times FY2019. Profit has not followed. Consolidated profit after tax for FY2022 to FY2026 was ₹4.65 crore, ₹3.62 crore, ₹3.32 crore, ₹1.33 crore and ₹5.33 crore, a five-year total of ₹18.25 crore on ₹430 crore of cumulative revenue [34][33][32][31][27].

Here is the FY2026 margin bridge per ₹100 of consolidated revenue. Purchases of traded software, net of stock change, cost ₹14.5. Employees cost ₹24.8. Other expenses cost ₹36.5, a line that holds ₹9.4 of credit-loss provision (₹12.49 crore) and, in the parent, ₹22.24 crore of outsourced technical consultants, up from ₹13.96 crore [27]. What remains is EBITDA of ₹24.2, or ₹32.19 crore, which is earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation. Depreciation and amortisation take ₹17.2. Interest takes ₹3.1. Other income adds ₹2.7. Pre-tax profit is ₹6.7. The feed's waterfall tells the same story in rounded form [37].

The margin did not improve in eight years. EBITDA margin was 25% in FY2019 and 24% in FY2026 [37]. What changed is below that line. Depreciation and amortisation rose from ₹4 crore, about 6% of revenue, in FY2019 to ₹22.8 crore, 17%, in FY2026, so pre-tax margin fell from about 17% to 6.7% [37][27]. Interest is the smaller drag. Finance cost was ₹4.07 crore in FY2026: ₹3.18 crore on borrowings and ₹0.71 crore on lease liabilities in the parent [27]. EBITDA covers that 7.9 times. EBIT, which is EBITDA less depreciation and amortisation and before other income, covers it only 2.3 times.

Why does amortisation keep climbing? SoftTech writes its own software, the Civit suite for building permits, infrastructure and construction. Under Ind AS 38 it capitalises eligible development cost, meaning it records the spend as an asset instead of an expense, and amortises it straight-line over four years once the product is available for use. Until then the money sits in 'intangible assets under development' [27]. The auditor makes this a key audit matter 'due to the significant value of the development costs', and the notes concede that 'there is significant management judgement and estimate involved' in deciding which costs qualify [27]. In FY2026 ₹36.48 crore went into the under-development account, ₹33.05 crore moved into finished software and ₹20.43 crore of internally generated software was amortised [27]. Put those next to EBITDA and you see how much of 'operating profit' is really re-invested engineering.

Read the last column with care. It is a sensitivity, not a restatement. Some capitalised cost is genuine asset-building, and the notes do not split capitalised salary from contractor cost, so I cannot say how much would have been an expense in a stricter regime. But the direction is clear: in FY2024, FY2025 and FY2026 the group would have reported a pre-tax loss had it expensed development as it went. Cash tells the same tale. Across FY2022 to FY2026 the group paid ₹117.16 crore for intangibles against cumulative EBITDA of ₹110.45 crore [34][33][32][31][27].

And the pile is growing. Software under development rose from ₹19.56 crore in March 2026 to ₹42.66 crore in September 2026, while finished software fell from ₹70.65 crore to ₹58.18 crore [27][30]. If that ₹42.66 crore entered service on a four-year life it would add about ₹10.7 crore a year of amortisation, against Q2 FY2027 EBITDA of ₹7.98 crore for the quarter and depreciation and amortisation already at ₹6.85 crore [30]. That is arithmetic, not a forecast: it assumes no new revenue from those products. It is why I watch the amortisation line more closely than the EBITDA line.

Look at what the March 2026 balance sheet holds. Total consolidated assets are ₹253.54 crore. Capitalised software is ₹70.65 crore, software under development ₹19.56 crore, trade receivables ₹34.63 crore and unbilled contract assets ₹53.52 crore. Those four lines are ₹178.4 crore, 70% of everything the group owns [27]. Plant and equipment is just ₹3.62 crore. This is an asset-light business whose assets are code and promises of payment. Goodwill is nil: the only goodwill ever created, ₹0.16 crore on buying the German company, was written off in full in the year of purchase [27].

Investments tell a second story. The parent has put about ₹28.1 crore into subsidiaries, ₹13.7 crore of equity and ₹14.4 crore of optionally convertible debentures [27]. In FY2026 it injected ₹11.25 crore into SoftTech Digital AG, the German company, which in its first months produced no revenue and a ₹0.63 crore loss [27]. Provisions of ₹0.74 crore already sit against subsidiary investments, mostly the Finland debentures [27]. A loss that never touched profit also deserves a mention: the parent's stake in QI Square Singapore was marked down from ₹4.60 crore to ₹1.29 crore, a ₹3.31 crore hit taken through other comprehensive income and so absent from the profit figures above [27]. One consolidation quirk too. Group cash of ₹12.71 crore at March 2026 looks like a ₹10.1 crore rise, but the parent held only ₹1.16 crore. The German subsidiary has ₹10.57 crore of assets against ₹11.35 crore of share capital, so the 'increase' is mostly money moved from the parent's fixed deposits to Germany, not new cash [27].

Gross debt barely moved, ₹34.4 crore to ₹31.7 crore, but look at the mix. Seventy-two percent (₹22.93 crore) is bank working-capital lines secured on receivables and stock and backed by personal guarantees and equitable mortgages on the managing director's and his wife's flats [27]. ₹3.02 crore is loans from those two directors at 10%. The non-bank lenders charge about 11.25%, bank lines 7.7% to 10.25% [27]. So the group pays 8% to 11% for money it needs mainly because customers pay slowly. Net of liquid funds it had ₹4.06 crore of net cash at March 2026 before leases and ₹3.03 crore of net debt after them; by September 2026 liquid funds of ₹28.06 crore were below borrowings of ₹32.12 crore [27][30]. Two debt-like items sit outside that table: ₹13.43 crore owed to suppliers for capital purchases, up from ₹7.90 crore, and ₹6.22 crore of fixed deposits pledged to lenders [27]. Contingent liabilities, disputes not provided for, total ₹5.10 crore: ₹3.63 crore of income-tax demands (chiefly a ₹2.75 crore reopening of assessment year 2018-19), ₹1.39 crore of GST and ₹0.08 crore other. Management expects no material cash outflow [27].

Now the part that matters most. Receivables come in two pieces. Trade receivables are invoices already sent. Contract assets, also called unbilled revenue, are revenue booked under percentage-of-completion accounting but not yet invoiced. Add them and you get what customers owe or will owe: ₹88.15 crore at March 2026 on ₹132.90 crore of revenue, or 242 days. That is down from 628 days in FY2021 and 366 in FY2025 [34][31][27]. Management's own figure for the standalone company is 260 days, down from 462 in FY2022, and the annual report sets a goal of 'bringing DSO below 200 days' [27]. The feed's 95 debtor days covers trade receivables alone and misses the larger half. Its cash-conversion cycle of minus 256 and minus 108 days for FY2025 and FY2026 is an artefact of netting a large payables balance against a small purchases base; ignore it [37].

Who owes it? The filings do not split receivables between government bodies and private customers. The annual report says only that revenue is 'concentrated in a single customer type (government)' [27], and I could not size that exposure. What is disclosed: ₹1.79 crore is owed by the Dubai subsidiary, up from ₹0.74 crore [27]. A municipality that approves a budget in one year and pays in the next is slow money, and the ageing below shows it.

The ageing is the uncomfortable part. Of ₹40.83 crore of gross trade receivables, ₹17.28 crore (42%) is more than a year old and ₹4.97 crore is older than three years. The allowance covers 72% of the oldest bucket but only 12% of the one-to-two-year bucket, so cover on everything over a year is 31% [27]. On the unbilled side there is ₹64.89 crore of gross contract assets with an ₹11.37 crore loss allowance, up from ₹2.04 crore. Together the group holds ₹17.65 crore of allowances against ₹105.72 crore of billed and unbilled claims, 16.7%, up from ₹5.16 crore a year earlier [27]. The FY2026 charge of ₹12.49 crore compares with consolidated pre-tax profit of ₹8.93 crore. Bad debt is not new: the annual reports show write-offs of ₹0.92 crore in FY2018 and ₹0.37 crore in FY2021 [36][35]. What is new is the scale, and the timing: parent other expenses jumped to ₹24.80 crore in Q4 against ₹7.87 crore in Q3 [28].

Returns on capital are the verdict on all of this. The feed's ROCE, operating profit after depreciation over capital employed, was 13% in FY2020 and 6% in FY2026, with 4% in FY2025 [37]. Here is my own version for FY2026, consolidated. EBIT of ₹9.36 crore (pre-tax profit plus interest, less other income), taxed at the 25.17% statutory rate, gives net operating profit after tax of ₹7.01 crore. Invested capital, meaning equity plus borrowings plus leases less cash and liquid funds, averages ₹171.0 crore. Return on invested capital is 4.1%. Add back the credit-loss charge and it is 9.6% [27]. The company's own lenders charge 7.7% to 11.25%, so a 4.1% return does not cover even the cost of debt. A sensible hurdle for the equity of a small Indian software company is 12% to 15%; that is my assumption, not a filed number. Return on equity was 2.9% on owners' equity (management quotes 3.1% on total equity, and 5.2% for the parent alone) [27], and the feed puts the three-year average near 2.1% [37].

Cash flow is where the story turns. Consolidated operating cash flow was ₹31.26 crore in FY2026, nearly six times profit after tax and 97% of EBITDA [27]. Do not applaud yet. Operating cash flow is struck before the cash spent on software development, which the accounts file under investing. Subtract that and free cash flow, operating cash less money spent on equipment and capitalised development, was minus ₹1.30 crore. The feed shows free cash flow negative in every one of the eight years from FY2019 to FY2026, adding to about minus ₹46 crore [37]. Warren Buffett wrote in Berkshire Hathaway's 2000 annual report: 'References to EBITDA make us shudder - does management think the tooth fairy pays for capital expenditures?' Capitalised software is that question in a new costume.

The bridge shows what lifted FY2026 operating cash. The ₹12.98 crore credit-loss add-back is 28% of cash earnings before working capital; it is not cash, but it is also a confession that earlier revenue did not convert. Working capital then absorbed ₹10.46 crore: trade receivables released ₹5.60 crore, but contract assets and stock absorbed ₹12.72 crore and payables fell ₹7.13 crore [27]. After the ₹3.44 crore of interest and ₹1.79 crore of lease payments that sit in financing, the shortfall was ₹6.5 crore. The group met it by redeeming a net ₹15.7 crore of fixed deposits, which had been built up in FY2025 when the December 2024 equity issue came in [27]. In the first half of FY2027 operating cash was ₹15.86 crore against ₹22.08 crore spent on development and equipment, a ₹6.23 crore shortfall (₹11.05 crore a year earlier), and the group drew ₹8.92 crore of new term loans [30].

Who funded the gap? Over FY2022 to FY2026, EBITDA of ₹110.45 crore became ₹96.92 crore of operating cash, 88%. The group then spent ₹122.92 crore on development and equipment, a ₹26.0 crore hole before ₹20.33 crore of finance cost. New shareholder money was ₹83.35 crore. Borrowings did not fund it: consolidated debt was ₹32.08 crore at March 2021 and ₹31.74 crore at March 2026 [34][27]. Customers certainly did not. They are the ones being funded, to the tune of ₹88 crore of unpaid claims. The growth of the last five years was paid for by outside equity investors.

Now per-share arithmetic. Shares outstanding rose from 94,22,476 at the 2018 listing to 1,38,42,138 today, up 47% [36][27]. Consolidated earnings per share in the feed went from ₹7.87 in FY2019 to ₹3.57 in FY2026 [37][27]. Outside investors put in ₹102.3 crore of new equity across the IPO and three placements, while the group earned about ₹34 crore in total over FY2019 to FY2026 on the feed's rounded figures [37]. Where did the issue proceeds go? The statement of deviation says nothing was diverted from the stated objects. Of ₹83.30 crore received across the 2021, 2022 and 2024 issues, ₹68.54 crore was used by March 2026: ₹55.77 crore 'to support the expansion of business in Indian and Overseas market' and ₹12.78 crore for general purposes, with ₹14.76 crore left in mutual funds and fixed deposits [27]. By June 2026 ₹33.14 crore of the ₹33.29 crore 2022 issue was used and ₹26.17 crore of the ₹40.01 crore 2024 issue [29]. 'Expansion' is broad enough to cover capitalised software, and the filings do not break it down. For the 2021 issue the early record is specific: by March 2022 ₹2.54 crore of ₹4.47 crore spent had gone to Civit development [34].

The owners behind the share count have changed. Promoter holding was 32.05% in March 2024, 20.35% in June 2024 and 18.89% since December 2024 [37]. The fall followed a June 2024 agreement under which Vijay Gupta, Udyat Indian Ventures LLP and Covisible Solutions sold 25,00,000 shares, 19.5%, to Einstein Work Pte Ltd, which then also took part of the December 2024 issue [31]. Einstein holds 23.41% today [27]. I found no pledge of promoter shares in the annual report or the feed. What is pledged is ₹6.22 crore of bank deposits and the promoters' personal flats and guarantees for bank lines [27]. Stock options are small: ESOP expense was ₹0.78 crore in FY2026 and ₹1.34 crore in FY2025, and 4,200 options at ₹10 were granted to the new chief financial officer in June 2026 [27][30]. The FY2026 option table does not roll forward cleanly: 60,000 opening plus 35,000 granted less 35,000 shares issued is not the 25,000 reported [27].

Governance deserves a plain list. The auditor, P G Bhagwat LLP, has served since the 30 September 2021 annual meeting [34]. It gave unmodified opinions with two key audit matters for FY2026: revenue on fixed-price contracts and capitalised development cost, the latter marked as a key matter 'for the current year' [27]. The Board reports no qualifications or adverse remarks [27]. The audit report on legal requirements does contain a notable item. Quarterly statements filed with the working-capital banks did not agree with the books: for March 2026 the composite of contract assets, receivables, payables, purchases and sales was ₹240.19 crore in the bank return against ₹256.14 crore in the books, and the December 2025 return ran ₹12.35 crore above the books. Management calls the returns provisional and says it will resubmit if permitted [27]. The secretarial auditor notes one late transfer of ₹10,000 of unpaid dividend to the investor protection fund, 125 days late [27].

Related-party and people items. The managing director drew ₹81.00 lakh of salary, ₹62.22 lakh of non-compete fees and ₹29.81 lakh of interest on his loan to the company in FY2026, ₹1.73 crore in all, equal to 32% of consolidated profit after tax [27]. Another executive director's pay rose from ₹14.46 lakh to ₹80.71 lakh [27]. The chief financial officer resigned in September 2025, a new one joined the next day, and the company secretary resigned in March 2026 [27]. The related-party note lists seven directors, four of them independent, with the managing director also chairman and chief executive [27]. None of this is alarming on its own. Together with the bank-return mismatch, the heavy loss allowance and a new key audit matter, it says controls are still catching up with the company's growth.

So what is the earnings quality, in plain words? Reported profit is thin and soft: ₹5.33 crore on ₹132.90 crore of revenue in FY2026, after a ₹12.49 crore credit-loss charge, and a loss if development spend were expensed. The cash is real at the operating line, where EBITDA converts at 88% to 97% over five years, but every rupee of it and more goes back into building software, so free cash flow is negative year after year. Revenue turns into cash slowly (242 days) and, for a growing slice, not at all. The business is funded by new shareholders, not by customers or lenders. Returns, 4.1% on my arithmetic, are below the cost of money. What would change my mind is two or three consecutive years of positive free cash flow with days outstanding under 200, falling allowances and amortisation growing slower than revenue.

Picture a municipal engineer in a mid-sized Maharashtra city. A builder submits a plan, the engineer opens a screen, the software checks the drawing against the rules, and an approval number comes out in days instead of weeks. SoftTech books revenue as plans are approved or transactions are processed, and the city is billed later. Some months later a finance officer in the municipality processes the bill, subject to a budget line and a sign-off. That gap between 'work done' and 'cash received' is the 242 days in this chapter. Now picture the other side: a team of engineers in Pune writing the next version of the product, paid every month in cash, with the cost put on the balance sheet instead of the profit statement. Both facts sit in the same accounts, and they pull in opposite directions.

If I were across the table from the finance chief, I would ask five things. Which customers make up the ₹17.28 crore of trade receivables older than a year, and are they governments or developers? What exactly was written down in Q4 FY2026, and why then? How much of the ₹36.48 crore capitalised in FY2026 was salary and how much was contractor fees? When will the ₹42.66 crore now under development start earning, and what amortisation should I model? And why did the March 2026 bank return understate the books by ₹15.95 crore in composite terms? The answers matter more than any quarterly profit.

An old accounting saying has it that profit is an opinion and cash is a fact. SoftTech is a useful case because both are visible at once. The opinion, ₹5.33 crore, rests on judgements about which engineering costs are assets and which revenue will be collected. The facts, ₹31.26 crore of operating cash and ₹30.50 crore paid to developers, are harder to argue with. Buffett's tooth-fairy line about EBITDA exists precisely for companies where the cost of staying in business hides below the operating line.

Here is the one-paragraph recap. SoftTech's revenue has tripled since FY2021. Its operating margin has been about a quarter of sales the whole time. Almost all of that margin is being re-spent on building software, which then shows up as rising amortisation. Customers pay in eight months or more, so the group borrows from banks and promoters and, above all, raises equity. The last five years consumed ₹83 crore of new equity to produce about ₹18 crore of profit. The product investments may well pay off, since an installed base of permit systems is sticky, but the numbers so far describe a business that is building, not yet harvesting.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: The two profit numbers people quote, ₹5.33 crore consolidated and ₹9.57 crore standalone, are both correct and neither is the whole story. The deeper facts are that the business turns roughly every rupee of EBITDA back into capitalised software, that customers take about eight months to pay, and that outside equity has paid for the last five years of growth. The next proof point is not a bigger revenue line; it is a year of positive free cash flow with the receivable days below 200.
